nature-pol-305.title: Biodiesel: fuel from oils and fats
nature-pol-305.text: Biodiesel is the most common biofuel in Europe. It is made from oils or fats by a chemical process called transesterification, and its composition is close to fossil diesel, mostly fatty acid methyl or ethyl esters. Feedstocks range from animal fats and soy to rapeseed, jatropha, palm oil and algae. The IEA estimated that in 2021 biodiesel production used 17% of global vegetable oil supplies. Palm oil proved the problem crop: unsustainable farming of it has caused deforestation and pollution, so the European Commission approved a measure to phase out palm oil-based biofuels by 2030.

nature-pol-307.title: Biogas from waste and energy crops
nature-pol-307.text: Biogas is what microorganisms produce when they digest organic material without oxygen. It is mostly methane and carbon dioxide. The feed can be biodegradable waste, or energy crops added to anaerobic digesters, which are sealed tanks, to raise the gas yield. A biodigester can process manure, food waste, agricultural residues, fats, oils and wastewater solids. What is left, the digestate, can serve as fertilizer or soil amendment.

nature-pol-304.title: Ethanol fuel from sugar and grain
nature-pol-304.text: Ethanol is the most common biofuel worldwide, especially in Brazil. It is an alcohol made by fermenting sugars or starches, or the tougher cellulose, with microorganisms and enzymes. The crops it uses are also food. The IEA estimated that in 2021 ethanol took 20% of sugar supplies and 13% of corn supplies. Up to 40% of US corn is turned into ethanol, and worldwide about 10% of all grain is made into biofuel.

nature-pol-313.title: Smart growth: planning against sprawl
nature-pol-313.text: Smart growth favors mixed-use, closely spaced development over sprawl. The term is used mainly in North America; "compact city" and "urban intensification" describe similar ideas in Europe, especially the UK, where they have shaped policy. The American Planning Association and Smart Growth America favor buildings near one another to cut car use. Maryland's 1997 Smart Growth Areas Act directed funding to areas already growing or with development plans. Does density work? Melia and colleagues (2011) found that raising it does reduce car use, but weakly: doubling density will not halve how often or how far people drive.

nature-pol-312.title: Is urban sprawl a problem or a preference?
nature-pol-312.text:
Sources call the cause, costs and remedies of sprawl contested. Critics argue it creates more problems than it solves and should be regulated. Proponents argue that markets produce the most economically efficient settlements. Peter Gordon says most households have shown a clear preference for low-density living, though whether sprawl reflects that preference is itself disputed.

Some worry that anti-sprawl policy raises housing prices. Evidence on Oregon is mixed: one study found the largest affordability loss, another found Portland's rises similar to other Western cities. Many critics concede that sprawl creates negative externalities but dispute the cure. Gordon and Richardson argue that new transit costs outweigh its benefits and that land-use limits raise housing costs.

nature-pol-310.title: Critical habitat under the Endangered Species Act
nature-pol-310.text: Critical habitat is a legal designation under the US Endangered Species Act for areas essential to conserving a listed species, even if the species does not live there yet. It is weaker than it sounds. It creates no preserve or refuge and does not bar development; it affects only federal agency actions, such as federally funded activities or those needing a federal permit. Under Section 7, those agencies must ensure their actions do not jeopardize a listed species or destroy or adversely modify its critical habitat. Before designating, agencies must weigh economic and national security impacts, and an area may be excluded if exclusion benefits outweigh designation benefits, unless exclusion would cause extinction. Good designations need detailed population and ecological data, and a compromise between protection and economic needs.

nature-pol-179.title: Performance and technology standards compared
nature-pol-179.text:
Most direct pollution rules come in two forms, and the difference is who chooses the equipment. A performance standard is a numeric limit, typically measured at the discharge point, and the facility may meet it with any technology it likes. Regulators often base the limit on a model technology, as US EPA does for industrial wastewater. Examples include the US New Source Performance Standards for new industrial facilities and EU CO2 performance standards for new cars.

A technology standard dictates the equipment itself. Its virtue is easy monitoring and enforcement: a regulator can check a car's design for a catalytic converter, which is why lawmakers often control tools rather than behavior. Its weakness is that it gives no incentive to change other behavior, such as miles driven, and it can backfire. Early water-efficient toilets led people to flush repeatedly. The Cabezas text calls technology standards the worst tool for promoting innovation, because firms are forbidden to use any other technology, even a cheaper one.

Letting firms choose how to meet the limit makes performance standards slightly more efficient. Still, both are less cost-effective than cap and trade, because the burden of cutting emissions cannot shift to firms that can cut more cheaply.

nature-pol-319.title: Economic spillover across regions and borders
nature-pol-319.text: An economic spillover is an impact, positive or more often negative, felt in one region or across the world because of an independent event elsewhere. Some spillovers pass through firms and households: an oil shortage raises fuel prices. Externality spillovers differ, being social costs not reflected in price without intervention. A rendering plant's odours are negative; a neighbour's garden is positive. Mill is credited with arguing that government intervention can prevent or mitigate them, whereas Adam Smith favoured a lightly regulated competitive market. They are hard to quantify, since health costs from pollution or the value of clean water lack direct market values. Globalisation makes them likelier, and trade with advanced economies can bring positive technology and investment spillovers.

nature-pol-316.title: Auction theory: how bidders behave
nature-pol-316.text: Auction theory studies how bidders behave in auctions and how auction features lead to predictable outcomes. Sellers use it to raise revenue and buyers to procure at lower cost, and theorists design auction rules to head off market failure. They treat an auction as a game with two aspects: its format, meaning the rules for prices, bids, closing and picking the winner, and the information bidders hold. Most bidders keep some private information from competitors, so information asymmetry shapes bidding. In the benchmark model each bidder has a private valuation, usually drawn independently from a probability distribution, and payment depends only on the bids. A bid function maps a buyer's value or a seller's cost to a bid price.

nature-econ-009.title: The revenue equivalence theorem
nature-econ-009.text: Under certain conditions, very different auctions pay the seller the same. That is Vickrey's 1961 result, the revenue equivalence theorem: a large class of auctions all give the same expected revenue, the best the seller can get. His first proof covered two buyers with uniformly distributed values. Riley and Samuelson proved a much more general version in 1979, published in 1981. With independent, identically distributed private valuations, they showed any auction allocates the item to the highest bidder, and that allocation equivalence implies payoff equivalence for all reserve prices. It needs buyers with independent types from a continuous distribution, and an auction that sells to the buyer who values the good most.

nature-pol-320.title: Three ways to measure trade spillovers
nature-pol-320.text: Three families of methods assess trade-related spillovers. Multi-regional input-output analysis combines harmonised input-output tables with trade statistics. It is easy to run across countries but uses average impacts, so it suits country-level sector analysis. Life-cycle assessments work bottom-up on individual products, the opposite of top-down input-output, and are less suitable for spillovers. Material-flow analyses track specific material flows along supply chains and across countries, mainly for raw commodities, and share the truncation problem of life-cycle assessment.

nature-pol-317.title: The simultaneous multiple-round auction
nature-pol-317.text: Selling telecommunication frequency slots posed a problem for the US Federal Communications Commission. Selling all slots by a traditional method would eventually either give licenses away for free or leave a telecom monopoly. The simultaneous multiple-round auction was deemed to solve it. Invented by Milgrom and Wilson, it combines the benefits of open English-style bidding and sealed bids. Paul Milgrom and Robert Wilson won the 2020 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for advancing auction theory with new formats, including this one.

nature-pol-318.title: Renewable energy certificates in the United States
nature-pol-318.text:
A renewable energy certificate is a tradable, non-tangible certificate proving that one megawatt-hour of electricity came from an eligible renewable source and was fed into the grid. Compliance markets arise from renewable portfolio standards in 29 states, DC and Puerto Rico, where utilities buy certificates to prove they supply the required share. Voluntary markets serve customers who choose renewable power. Prices vary with vintage year, location, supply and demand, compliance use and power type. Spot prices for solar certificates generally fell from 2010 to 2014; in New Jersey one went from $665.04 in July 2010 to about $160 in May 2014.

The US has no national registry. Regional registries and Green-e audits aim to prevent double counting, though critics say it still lets two parties claim one credit. Additionality means a purchase brings new renewable energy beyond business as usual; critics call it a subsidy.
